speaker: Patient
text: 59-year-old male. The patient presents to the emergency department with a sudden-onset sensation that the room is spinning, leading to several episodes of nausea and vomiting. The symptoms started as he was going to bed and lasted for approximately 3 minutes. He mentions that he has never experienced anything like this before and currently feels at his baseline.

speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you for the details. Since the episode was brief and you are now back to baseline, did you notice any severe headache, double vision, difficulty swallowing, or weakness in your limbs during those three minutes? Also, do you have a history of high blood pressure or recent neck pain?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Sudden-onset sensation of the room spinning. I also have Nausea, Vomiting, Dizziness. A doctor I saw earlier said this was very likely Gastroenteritis and told me the presentation was already quite typical.

speaker: Doctor
text:
The doctor notes your history of vomiting but clarifies that a previous diagnosis of gastroenteritis is unlikely given your primary symptom of spinning vertigo without fever or abdominal pain. Did the spinning sensation occur only when you moved your head or eyes, and do you currently have ringing in your ears or a feeling of fullness in your ear?

speaker: Doctor
text: DIAGNOSIS READY: Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV). The clinical presentation of brief, recurrent spinning vertigo triggered by position changes, without auditory symptoms or neurological deficits, is classic for BPPV, likely caused by otoconia displacement in the posterior semicircular canal. The normal hearing test and lack of stroke signs further support this diagnosis.
